dataset_name: Sparkov simulated credit-card fraud transactions — original fraudTest.csv portion

source.download_method: Native git read of public repository commit; exact archive bytes saved outside app repository

independent_corroboration.evidence: Independently hosted Git-LFS pointer identifies identical SHA256 and byte size as downloaded ZIP

scope.original_portion: fraudTest.csv only; original fraudTrain.csv not used
scope.project_usage: This publicly available portion is repurposed into new chronological training, validation, and test partitions for this project.
scope.historical_claims: Do not claim evaluation on the original published train/test split, or on the full approximately 1.85 million-row combined dataset.

checks: ZIP CRC; explicit single-member safe extraction
555719 rows and both binary target classes
No missing values or nonfinite numeric values
Unique transaction identifiers; no duplicated full rows
Archive SHA256 independently corroborated by separate public Git-LFS pointer
rejected_inputs: Empty 22-byte ZIP mirror archives were not used
Already encoded gzipped CSV without raw account IDs was not used
Unretrieved Git-LFS original train data was not used

limitations: All cardholder identities, account numbers, merchants, transactions, and fraud labels are simulated; this is an academic demonstration.
Synthetic generator rules can make fraud unusually predictable; strong scores do not establish real-bank deployment performance.
Chronological evaluation of accounts with past history demonstrates future transactions for known accounts; it does not establish performance on unseen accounts.
Only the original fraudTest.csv source portion was available and audited, and it is newly split within this project.

Dataset license was not independently verified against the canonical Kaggle page because environment egress blocked access; a third-party README describes CC0, which is not treated here as verified licensing metadata.

The provided unix_time is consistently offset by 220924800 seconds from trans_date_trans_time interpreted as UTC. Use the human-readable transaction datetime consistently for model time/history features; avoid treating the raw unix_time as the actual 2020 timestamp.
